title: PhD in Real-Time LLM-Based Distributed Autonomy for Safety-Critical Autonomous Driving (AIDA)
summary: Small language models for real-time planning, shared fleet memory and safety-aware distributed vehicle coordination.
tasks: Investigate real-time edge reasoning with compact small language models.
Design selective fleet episodic memory and experience retrieval.
Study communication-aware distributed planning and safe fallback mechanisms.
Evaluate in simulation and on RoboRacer platforms.
background: Master’s degree or equivalent in a relevant field.
Strong background in control, machine learning, autonomous systems or related methods.
subject: Application — AIDA PhD

sections.heading: The position
paragraphs: Within the AIDA project (AI-Driven Distributed Autonomy, FWF), you will investigate how Small Language Models (SLMs) can support real-time high-level planning and coordination in safety-critical autonomous driving systems — combining distributed AI planning, communication-aware coordination, and safety-aware integration with vehicle control.A key focus is experience-based autonomy: instead of storing all data, vehicles selectively retain novel, surprising, or safety-relevant episodes in a shared fleet memory. Similar past cases are then retrieved to support decisions in unfamiliar situations.Research directions include: real-time edge reasoning with compact SLMs; selective fleet episodic memory design; distributed planning under communication constraints; and timing/safety analysis with runtime monitoring and safe fallback mechanisms. Evaluation will use simulation and TU Wien autonomous platforms (RoboRacer), with potential extension to full-scale vehicle experiments.

sections.heading: Appointment and supervision
paragraphs: Duration: 30 months. Working time: 40h/week. Start: To be confirmed.
Supervisor: Ezio Bartocci. Co-supervisor: Agnes Poks — Project PI (TU Wien).

subject: Thesis enquiry — Surface-Aware Minimum-Time Raceline Optimization on Three-Dimensional Tracks

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Extending the existing two-dimensional optimizer with elevation, banking, gravity, and geometry-dependent vehicle limits

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: The current raceline-generation tool represents the track in two dimensions. This is appropriate for a nearly planar surface, but it cannot represent elevation changes, banking, off-camber turns, or the resulting changes in gravity and normal load. These effects alter the feasible acceleration envelope and may change both the optimal path and speed profile.

With a 3D LiDAR and an appropriate mapping pipeline, the track can instead be represented as a three-dimensional road. This thesis investigates how such a representation can be incorporated into the existing raceline optimizer. The work should build directly on the current implementation and be compared with the three-dimensional racing-planning tools developed at the Technical University of Munich.
Objective and Scope: The goal is to extend the existing raceline optimizer to compute dynamically feasible minimum-time trajectories on a track with measurable elevation or banking.

sections.heading: Tasks
paragraphs: Review and document the existing raceline implementation together with its original developer.
Derive a suitable 3D track representation containing centerline position, width, elevation, local orientation, curvature, and banking.
Extend the vehicle constraints and optimization formulation to account for gravity projection and geometry-dependent acceleration limits.
Compare the resulting method with the current 2D optimizer and an available TUM three-dimensional racing-line implementation.
Validate the approach on controlled non-planar track sections in simulation and, where practical, on the 1:10 platform.

sections.heading: Expected Outcome
paragraphs: A documented extension of the existing raceline tool from planar to surface-aware optimization.
A quantitative analysis of when three-dimensional track geometry materially changes the optimal path, speed profile, or lap time.
A reusable interface between 3D track mapping and raceline optimization; a convincing experimental comparison has publication potential.

sections.heading: Student Profile
paragraphs: Background in mechanical engineering, control, robotics, or computational engineering.
Understanding of vehicle dynamics, optimal control, and numerical optimization.
Python, MATLAB, CasADi, or C++ experience; knowledge of differential geometry is useful but not required.

sections.heading: 1:10 Testbed and Scope Boundary
paragraphs: A track with controlled elevation or banking must be available or constructed; otherwise, the difference from the 2D formulation may be too small to evaluate meaningfully. The thesis studies one road-surface representation and the existing vehicle model. A full multibody vehicle model, general off-road planning, and online multi-vehicle trajectory planning are outside the scope.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Building globally consistent point-cloud and road-surface maps under high speed, vibration, scan distortion, and repeated track geometry

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: The addition of a 3D LiDAR enables the vehicle to capture track elevation, banking, barriers, and surrounding geometry that cannot be represented by the current 2D map. These maps could support 3D localization, surface-aware raceline optimization, visualization, and improved perception.

Modern LiDAR–inertial mapping systems provide a strong starting point, but racing introduces difficult conditions: rapid rotations, vibration, motion distortion, limited onboard compute, and tracks containing repeated geometric structures. Rather than developing an entirely new SLAM system, this thesis benchmarks established methods and introduces one clearly motivated racing-specific improvement.
Objective and Scope: The goal is to produce accurate and repeatable 3D track maps and a usable road-surface representation from the vehicle’s 3D LiDAR and inertial measurements.

sections.heading: Tasks

Characterize failure sources including motion distortion, vibration, low-feature sections, repeated geometry, and loop-closure errors.
Implement one targeted improvement, such as racing-aware deskewing, sensor-quality weighting, constrained motion priors, or improved loop closure.
Evaluate map consistency, surface accuracy, repeatability, computational cost, and suitability for downstream raceline optimization.

sections.heading: Expected Outcome
paragraphs: A reproducible 3D mapping pipeline for the 1:10 racing platform.
Globally consistent point-cloud maps together with a road-surface or track-ribbon representation.
A quantitative comparison of established mapping systems and one racing-specific improvement; a carefully designed dataset and evaluation may support publication.

subject: Thesis enquiry — Optical Ground-Flow-Aided Sideslip Estimation and Feedback Control for Scaled Autonomous Racing

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Using downward-facing optical sensors to estimate lateral velocity and provide sideslip-aware MPC and raceline limits

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: Vehicle sideslip angle is an important indicator of operation near the tire-friction limit, but it cannot be measured directly using the standard onboard IMU and wheel-speed sensors. Model-based estimates can become inaccurate when tire or surface properties change—the same conditions in which sideslip information is most valuable.

Downward-facing optical-flow sensors offer a direct measurement of planar motion relative to the ground. The platform already has suitable sensors intended for mounting on the bottom plate. Their measurements are nevertheless affected by mounting height, pitch and roll, yaw rotation, surface texture, illumination, vibration, and intermittent loss of optical quality. This thesis investigates their use within a robust multi-sensor sideslip estimator and evaluates whether sideslip feedback improves control near the handling limits.

Objective and Scope: The goal is to estimate body-frame lateral velocity and sideslip in real time using optical ground-flow measurements and integrate the estimate into the existing MPC and raceline workflow.

sections.heading: Tasks
paragraphs: Mount, calibrate, and characterize the optical-flow sensors, including scale, orientation, lever-arm, height, and surface-dependent effects.
Develop a measurement model that compensates for rotational motion and changes in vehicle attitude.
Fuse optical flow with IMU, wheel-speed, steering, and vehicle-model information using an EKF, UKF, or moving-horizon estimator.
Validate lateral velocity and sideslip estimates against motion-capture or another suitable ground-truth system.
Integrate the estimate into the MPC and use experimental sideslip limits to refine the raceline optimizer’s dynamic constraints.

sections.heading: Expected Outcome
paragraphs: A calibrated optical ground-flow sensing system and reproducible sideslip-estimation pipeline.
A quantitative analysis of estimator accuracy, delay, failure conditions, and robustness across different surfaces and maneuvers.
Closed-loop evidence showing whether sideslip feedback improves stability, constraint handling, or lap performance; the sensor-fusion study has publication potential.

sections.heading: Your Profile
paragraphs: Background in mechanical engineering, control, mechatronics, or signal processing.
Understanding of vehicle dynamics and state estimation.
Python, MATLAB, embedded programming, or ROS experience; practical interest in sensor integration is desirable.

sections.heading: 1:10 Testbed and Scope Boundary
paragraphs: The thesis uses one defined optical-sensor installation and focuses on lateral velocity and sideslip estimation. It does not attempt to identify a complete tire-force model or spatial friction map. Controller integration is limited to selected sideslip-aware constraints or feedback terms in the existing MPC and raceline tool.

subject: Thesis enquiry — Batched GPU-Accelerated Nonlinear Model Predictive Control for Scaled Autonomous Racing

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: Nonlinear model predictive control can exploit tire limits and vehicle dynamics more effectively than simpler control methods, but its computational cost restricts prediction horizon, model complexity, and replanning frequency. GPU-native solvers such as TurboMPC introduce substantial parallelism and have already demonstrated demanding control applications, including full-scale racing.

This project investigates where GPU computation produces a measurable advantage on a resource-constrained 1:10 vehicle. Candidate benefits include batched multi-start optimization, parallel contingency trajectories, uncertainty scenarios, and longer prediction horizons. Particular attention is paid to solver latency distributions, CPU–GPU transfer overhead, power consumption, and closed-loop racing performance.

Objective and Scope: The goal is to design and evaluate a GPU-accelerated nonlinear MPC architecture that uses parallel optimization to improve racing performance without violating the vehicle’s real-time compute budget.

sections.heading: Tasks
paragraphs: Measure the existing CPU-based MPC as a verified baseline and define accuracy, timing, and closed-loop performance metrics.
Implement the racing model, constraints, and objective using TurboMPC or a comparable GPU-native optimization framework.
Investigate one or two GPU-specific strategies, preferably batched multi-start optimization, parallel uncertainty scenarios, or contingency trajectories.
Determine the break-even point between CPU and GPU execution as a function of horizon length, model complexity, and batch size.
Validate the resulting controller in simulation and through selected closed-loop experiments on the 1:10 vehicle.

sections.heading: Expected Outcome
paragraphs: A reproducible GPU-based MPC implementation for the existing autonomous racing platform.
A quantitative analysis of when GPU acceleration is beneficial for small-scale real-time control.

A closed-loop comparison covering lap time, tracking error, constraint violations, deadline misses, compute utilization, and energy use; a strong experimental study has conference-publication potential.

sections.heading: Student Profile
paragraphs: Background in control, robotics, computational engineering, or a related discipline.
Understanding of optimization and vehicle dynamics; Python, JAX, CUDA, or C++ experience is useful.
Interest in numerical algorithms and embedded GPU systems; prior GPU-programming experience is helpful but not mandatory.

sections.heading: 1:10 Testbed and Scope Boundary
paragraphs: The thesis uses the existing 1:10 RoboRacer/F1TENTH-scale platform and its simulation environment. It focuses on one established racing MPC formulation and a small number of GPU-specific parallelization strategies. Developing a general-purpose GPU optimizer, redesigning the complete autonomy stack, or benchmarking many unrelated solvers is outside the scope.

subject: Thesis enquiry — Latency-Aware RGB-D Obstacle Detection and Tracking for Scaled Autonomous Racing

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Fusing RGB semantics, depth geometry, and temporal information under the vehicle’s real-time compute budget

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: The current team platform uses a comparatively simple obstacle-detection method. While sufficient for controlled demonstrations, it may produce unreliable detections when obstacle appearance, depth quality, or vehicle motion changes. Missed detections are safety-critical, whereas excessive false positives can unnecessarily slow or stop the vehicle.

An RGB-D fusion strategy could provide complementary information: RGB data supports semantic recognition, while depth supports geometric separation from the ground and background. Effective fusion must account for calibration, synchronization, missing or noisy depth, motion blur, and the limited computational resources available onboard. For racing, end-to-end latency and temporal stability are as important as frame-level detection accuracy.

Objective and Scope: The goal is to develop an RGB-D obstacle-detection and tracking pipeline that improves reliability over the current method while satisfying a defined real-time latency budget on the vehicle.

sections.heading: Tasks
paragraphs: Define the target obstacle set and operating conditions, and collect or annotate a representative RGB-D evaluation dataset.
Calibrate and synchronize the RGB and depth streams and characterize depth failures during vehicle motion.
Implement efficient geometric proposals using depth, ground removal, clustering, or U-depth representations.
Compare RGB-only, depth-only, and selected early- or late-fusion approaches, including lightweight semantic classification or segmentation where useful.
Add temporal tracking and deploy the best pipeline onboard, evaluating detection range, recall, false positives, latency, and closed-loop behavior.

sections.heading: Expected Outcome
paragraphs: A reproducible and deployable RGB-D obstacle-detection pipeline for the 1:10 racing vehicle.
A quantitative comparison of RGB-only, depth-only, and fused perception under a fixed compute budget.
An annotated test set and latency-aware evaluation protocol; a well-scoped obstacle benchmark and fusion method may support publication.

sections.heading: Your Profile
paragraphs: Background in computer vision, robotics, embedded systems, or computational engineering.
Understanding of camera geometry, image processing, and machine learning.
Python, C++/ROS, or PyTorch experience; familiarity with ONNX or TensorRT is useful.

sections.heading: 1:10 Testbed and Scope Boundary
paragraphs: The thesis uses one RGB-D camera and one explicitly defined obstacle set, such as unexpected static track obstacles, opponent vehicles, or a carefully limited combination of both. It does not target general autonomous-driving perception, unrestricted object recognition, or full RGB-D and 3D-LiDAR fusion.

subject: Thesis enquiry — Failure-Aware Multi-Sensor Localization for High-Speed Scaled Autonomous Racing

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Combining racing-aware map matching, measurement-quality assessment, and global recovery beyond the current particle-filter/EKF pipeline

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: Reliable localization is essential for autonomous racing because small pose errors can cause large raceline-tracking errors near the handling limits. The current platform uses a particle filter together with an EKF-style state estimator. Although this solution is functional, wheel slip, high accelerations, repetitive track geometry, temporary sensor degradation, and incorrect initial poses can lead to overconfident or multimodal localization errors.

This thesis investigates whether a modernized localization architecture can improve accuracy and, more importantly, failure robustness. Candidate approaches include an improved racing-specific particle filter, fixed-lag smoothing or factor-graph fusion, adaptive measurement weighting, and explicit relocalization. BioSLAM is relevant as a lifelong place-recognition or relocalization component.

Objective and Scope: The goal is to develop a localization system that maintains accurate real-time pose estimates during normal racing and can recognize, contain, and recover from localization failures.

sections.heading: Tasks
paragraphs: Characterize the current particle-filter and EKF pipeline, including failure cases under wheel slip, high speed, sensor dropouts, and ambiguous track geometry.
Implement and compare selected alternatives such as an improved particle filter, fixed-lag smoother, or tightly coupled factor-graph estimator.
Develop measurement-quality or innovation-based checks that prevent unreliable observations from corrupting the state estimate.
Integrate a global relocalization mechanism using geometric place recognition and, where appropriate, concepts from BioSLAM.
Evaluate accuracy, recovery time, consistency, runtime, and closed-loop racing performance in simulation and on the 1:10 vehicle.

sections.heading: Expected Outcome
paragraphs: A modular and reproducible localization architecture tailored to scaled autonomous racing.
A quantitative comparison showing when the particle filter should be retained, improved, or complemented by smoothing and global recovery.
Demonstrated robustness to representative initialization errors, slip events, and sensor degradation; the resulting failure-oriented evaluation may support a conference publication.

sections.heading: Student Profile
paragraphs: Background in robotics, mechatronics, control, or computational engineering.
Knowledge of probabilistic estimation, coordinate transformations, and sensor fusion.
Python or C++/ROS experience; familiarity with particle filters, Kalman filters, or factor graphs is useful.

sections.heading: 1:10 Testbed and Scope Boundary
paragraphs: The thesis focuses on two-dimensional map-based racing localization using the existing sensor configuration and track maps. It does not include the construction of a full 3D map or the development of a new perception stack. Only a small number of estimator architectures will be investigated in depth.

subject: Thesis enquiry — Uncertainty-Aware Online Vehicle System Identification for Adaptive Autonomous Racing

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Continuously updating identifiable tire, actuator, and drivetrain parameters for raceline optimization and model predictive control

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: Accurate vehicle models are required for minimum-time raceline optimization and model predictive control. At present, model parameters are primarily identified before racing. Their validity can degrade during operation because of tire temperature and wear, changing friction, battery voltage, payload changes, actuator behavior, or minor modifications to the vehicle.

Online system identification could allow the autonomy stack to adapt to these changes. However, attempting to estimate too many correlated parameters can produce unstable or physically implausible models. Furthermore, parameter updates must be uncertainty-aware and must not destabilize the controller. This thesis therefore focuses on a deliberately small, identifiable parameter set and on safe interfaces between estimation, MPC, and raceline generation.

Objective and Scope: The goal is to estimate selected time-varying vehicle parameters during driving and use the estimates to improve prediction and control while maintaining physical plausibility and closed-loop safety.

sections.heading: Tasks
paragraphs: Analyze the existing vehicle model and select a small set of observable parameters, such as tire stiffness, friction-related limits, steering dynamics, drivetrain gain, or actuator delay.
Design informative but safe identification maneuvers and establish an offline reference-identification procedure.
Implement a recursive estimation method with uncertainty quantification, parameter bounds, excitation checks, and update gating.
Integrate fast parameter updates into the MPC and define a slower, controlled update mechanism for raceline or dynamic-envelope optimization.
Evaluate convergence, tracking of changing conditions, prediction accuracy, controller performance, and failure behavior in simulation and on the 1:10 vehicle.

sections.heading: Expected Outcome
paragraphs: A reproducible online system-identification pipeline for selected racing-vehicle parameters.
A quantitative answer to which parameters can be identified reliably during normal racing and how quickly they can be updated.
Demonstrated improvements in model prediction or closed-loop performance under at least one changing condition; a systematic estimator–controller study has publication potential.

sections.heading: Student Profile
paragraphs: Background in control, mechanical engineering, mechatronics, or computational engineering.
Understanding of vehicle dynamics, parameter estimation, and system identification.

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: Once a high-quality 3D map is available, the vehicle must localize within it accurately and with sufficiently low latency for racing control. Standard scan-to-map alignment can provide precise six-degree-of-freedom poses, but it may fail in geometrically repetitive areas, during aggressive motion, or when the initial pose is inaccurate.

A racing localization system must do more than report a pose. It should estimate whether the current alignment is trustworthy, avoid silently accepting incorrect matches, and recover globally when local tracking is lost. The known road surface and constrained vehicle motion can potentially improve both accuracy and robustness.

Objective and Scope: The goal is to develop a real-time 3D map-localization system that tracks the vehicle during racing, detects unreliable alignment, and recovers from initialization errors or localization loss.

Explicit confidence or failure indicators and demonstrated recovery from representative initialization and tracking failures.
A quantitative analysis of the benefit of road-surface constraints and global recovery; the failure-aware system has potential for a robotics publication.

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: A vehicle model calibrated under one condition can lose accuracy when the physical system changes. Typical causes include different tire-road friction, tire properties, payload, setup changes, or transfer to another nominally similar vehicle. Retraining a complete neural model from scratch ignores that most of the underlying physics remains unchanged and can require more data than is practical.

This thesis investigates data-efficient transfer of a hybrid physical-plus-Liquid vehicle model. Starting from a nominal physical model and a pretrained LRC/LrcSSM residual, one clearly defined physical change is introduced on the 1:10 platform. The student investigates which components should be adapted: interpretable physical parameters, the Liquid residual, or both. The project’s focus is on physical meaning, transfer efficiency, and closed-loop usefulness.
Objective and Scope

The goal is to determine how a physics-guided Liquid vehicle model can be transferred to a changed physical condition with minimal new data while maintaining prediction quality and control performance.

·        Compare adaptation strategies such as physical-parameter update only, Liquid-residual fine-tuning only, and a combined selective adaptation of both components.
·        Evaluate data efficiency, prediction error, physical consistency, generalization, and computation time for different amounts of target-condition data.
·        Validate the best adapted model with an existing predictive controller and selected closed-loop experiments on the 1:10 vehicle.

sections.heading: Expected Outcome
paragraphs: •         A reproducible physics-guided transfer-learning workflow for Liquid vehicle-dynamics models.
•         A quantitative answer to what should be transferred when one physical condition changes: physics, the Liquid residual, or both.
•         A data-efficient 1:10 validation; a systematic adaptation comparison has strong potential for a conference publication.

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: Accurate vehicle-dynamics models are essential for predictive control, especially close to the handling limits. Classical single-track models provide physical structure and interpretable parameters, but simplified tire assumptions and unmodeled actuator effects can reduce accuracy. Purely data-driven models can capture nonlinear effects, but they may require more data and generalize poorly outside the training range.

This thesis combines physical vehicle modeling with a compact Liquid Neural Network residual model. The focus is deliberately limited to lateral/yaw dynamics of the 1:10 autonomous car. A physical single-track model with a suitable tire representation is formulated and identified first. An MLP but also LRC /LrcSSM then learns only the remaining model mismatch. A simple conventional learned model can be used as a baseline. The resulting physics-informed Liquid model is evaluated both open-loop and inside an existing MPC/MPCC implementation.

Objective and Scope: The goal is to obtain an interpretable, control-oriented hybrid vehicle model that improves prediction beyond the physical baseline while retaining physical structure and real-time suitability. The approach will be parameterized and experimentally checked using data from the 1:10 autonomous car.

background: See the profile and scope in the topic description.
subject: Thesis enquiry — Diffusion-Based Behaviour Priors for MPCC in Autonomous Racing

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Generating multimodal follow, setup, overtake, and abort trajectories for 1:10 racing

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: Head-to-head autonomous racing requires more than accurate trajectory tracking. A racing vehicle must reason about the opponent, the local track geometry, and the tactical risk of a manoeuvre. In many situations, there is not a single correct solution: the vehicle may stay behind the opponent, prepare an overtake on the inside line, attack on the outside, delay the manoeuvre until the next straight, or abort because the available gap is too small. This makes overtaking a naturally multimodal decision-making problem.

Diffusion models are well suited for such problems because they can learn multimodal trajectory or action distributions from data. In robotics, Diffusion Policy has shown that action sequences can be generated through conditional denoising and executed in a receding-horizon manner. In autonomous driving, recent diffusion-based planners have demonstrated that diffusion models can generate diverse and high-quality driving trajectories under flexible guidance. However, for autonomous racing, especially on a 1:10 platform, safety and dynamic feasibility remain critical. Therefore, the diffusion model should not directly control steering and throttle.

This thesis investigates a diffusion-based tactical behaviour prior for Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC). The diffusion model generates short-horizon trajectory candidates for different manoeuvre modes, such as follow, setup-left, setup-right, overtake-left, overtake-right, and abort. These candidates are then used as warm starts or reference priors for an MPCC controller. The MPCC remains responsible for enforcing vehicle dynamics, track boundaries, actuator limits, collision avoidance, and progress maximization. The main research question is whether diffusion-generated behaviour priors can improve MPCC-based autonomous racing in interactive overtaking scenarios. The focus is not on replacing the controller with a black-box neural policy, but on using learning to provide better tactical initialization and multimodal manoeuvre suggestions for a constrained optimization-based controller.

sections.heading: Tasks
paragraphs: The student will generate a dataset of manoeuvre-conditioned racing trajectories in simulation. Each trajectory will be labelled as follow, setup-left, setup-right, overtake-left, overtake-right, or abort. A conditional diffusion model will be trained to generate short-horizon trajectory or control candidates for each manoeuvre class. The generated candidates will be used as warm starts/references for MPCC. The thesis should also investigate how many diffusion samples are needed for real-time operation on a 1:10 platform. If hardware tests are feasible, the final system should be evaluated at conservative speeds on the physical vehicle.

sections.heading: Expected Outcome
paragraphs: The expected outcome is a prototype of a diffusion-guided predictive controller for tactical autonomous racing. The thesis should show whether diffusion-generated candidates improve overtaking success, reduce failed attempts, or improve controller convergence. The most important result is not that diffusion directly drives the car, but that it provides better tactical priors for a safe downstream controller. Deliverables include a trajectory dataset, a trained conditional diffusion model, MPCC integration, and comparison against non-diffusion baselines.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Behaviour Learning for Safe Overtaking in 1:10 Autonomous Racing
summary: Learning interpretable tactical rules for opponent-aware control
tasks: The first task is to define a compact set of racing predicates in Frenet coordinates. These predicates should describe the local overtaking situation, including relative progress to the opponent, lateral position, available gap on the left and right side, track curvature, relative velocity, estimated time-to-collision, and whether the next track segment is suitable for overtaking. The second task is to implement a neural predicate estimator. This model should use recent ego and opponent state histories, local track information, and possibly LiDAR-based obstacle features to estimate soft truth values between 0 and 1. The third task is to implement a neuro-symbolic decision layer using a Logic Tensor Network, Logical Neural Network, or a related differentiable logic formulation.

The rules should not be treated as rigid hand-coded behaviour. Instead, they should act as differentiable priors that can be adjusted from data. The model should be trained using simulation data generated from rule-based controllers, MPCC rollouts, human demonstrations, or offline expert planners.

The fourth task is to connect the learned behaviour layer to an MPCC controller. The tactical output should modify controller parameters, for example the target lateral offset, progress weight, opponent-distance cost, risk budget, or abort behaviour. The low-level controller should remain responsible for producing dynamically feasible commands.

Finally, the method should be evaluated in simulation and, if feasible, on the 1:10 vehicle at conservative speeds. The evaluation should compare the neuro-symbolic behaviour layer against a purely rule-based strategy and a black-box neural behaviour classifier.

subject: Thesis enquiry — Neuro-Symbolic Behaviour Learning for Safe Overtaking in 1:10 Autonomous Racing

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Learning interpretable tactical rules for opponent-aware control

sections.heading: Background and Motivation
paragraphs: Autonomous racing is a compact but challenging benchmark for real-time decision making, prediction, and control. In head-to-head racing, the vehicle must not only follow a fast trajectory, but also reason about the behaviour of the opponent. A competitive racing vehicle should learn when to stay behind, when to prepare an overtaking manoeuvre, when to attack on the inside or outside line, and when to abort an unsafe attempt. Pure neural policies can learn such behaviours, but they are often difficult to interpret and validate. This is problematic for autonomous racing, where tactical decisions may lead to close interactions, blocking situations, or collisions. A promising alternative is a neuro-symbolic behaviour layer. In this approach, neural networks are used to estimate continuous predicates such as `gap_left_free`, `opponent_blocks_inside`, `ego_has_speed_advantage`, or `unsafe_time_to_collision`, while a differentiable logic model combines these predicates into tactical decisions.

The goal of this thesis is to develop a neuro-symbolic tactical behaviour layer for a 1:10 autonomous racing vehicle. The learned model should not directly output steering or throttle commands. Instead, it should select high-level manoeuvres such as `follow`, `pressure`, `setup-left`, `setup-right`, `overtake-left`, `overtake-right`, or `abort`. The selected manoeuvre is then executed by an  MPCC controller, which remains responsible for vehicle dynamics, trajectory generation, actuator limits, track boundaries, and safety constraints.

This separation is particularly suitable for 1:10 autonomous racing. The tactical decision can be made at a lower frequency and represented in an interpretable form, while the low-level controller runs in real time and handles the dynamic feasibility of the manoeuvre.

sections.heading: Tasks
paragraphs: The first task is to define a compact set of racing predicates in Frenet coordinates. These predicates should describe the local overtaking situation, including relative progress to the opponent, lateral position, available gap on the left and right side, track curvature, relative velocity, estimated time-to-collision, and whether the next track segment is suitable for overtaking. The second task is to implement a neural predicate estimator. This model should use recent ego and opponent state histories, local track information, and possibly LiDAR-based obstacle features to estimate soft truth values between 0 and 1. The third task is to implement a neuro-symbolic decision layer using a Logic Tensor Network, Logical Neural Network, or a related differentiable logic formulation.

The rules should not be treated as rigid hand-coded behaviour. Instead, they should act as differentiable priors that can be adjusted from data. The model should be trained using simulation data generated from rule-based controllers, MPCC rollouts, human demonstrations, or offline expert planners.

The fourth task is to connect the learned behaviour layer to an MPCC controller. The tactical output should modify controller parameters, for example the target lateral offset, progress weight, opponent-distance cost, risk budget, or abort behaviour. The low-level controller should remain responsible for producing dynamically feasible commands.

Finally, the method should be evaluated in simulation and, if feasible, on the 1:10 vehicle at conservative speeds. The evaluation should compare the neuro-symbolic behaviour layer against a purely rule-based strategy and a black-box neural behaviour classifier.

sections.heading: Expected Outcome
paragraphs: The expected result is an interpretable tactical decision-making module for 1:10 autonomous racing. The thesis should demonstrate that neuro-symbolic behaviour learning can predict useful manoeuvre decisions while preserving a clear connection to human-readable racing logic.

The final system should be able to decide when to follow, when to prepare an overtake, when to attack, and when to abort. The evaluation should include overtaking success rate, failed overtaking attempts, collision rate, track violations, minimum distance to the opponent, lap time, and decision interpretability.

A strong outcome would show that the neuro-symbolic model achieves similar or better performance than a black-box behaviour classifier while providing more interpretable tactical decisions. The thesis should also analyze which learned predicates and rules are most important for safe overtaking.

Your Profile: This topic is suitable for a student with an interest in machine learning, robotics, autonomous racing, and interpretable AI. Good Python skills are required. Experience with PyTorch, sequence models, reinforcement learning, or model predictive control is beneficial. Prior knowledge of formal logic is helpful but not mandatory. The student should be interested in combining learning-based methods with structured reasoning and experimental validation on a 1:10 autonomous vehicle.
